5-4.1 
Algae. 
The term “algae” refers to algal, microbiological, tiny, stringy blue and blue-green plants, 
which are usually found growing in masses on top of and on sides of cooling towers. 
Algae grow only in sunlit areas. They will slough off and become part of the suspended 
matter i

17191 bytes
n the circulating water, a situation which may cause fouling and plugging of 
water sprays. Algae also provide a breeding place, and are a nutrient, for bacteria. 
5-4.2 
Bacteria. 
The term “bacteria” refers to a large group of one-celled microorganisms. Bacteria can 
grow in either the absence or presence of sunlight. There are several ways to classify 
bacteria, including “aerobic,” meaning those living in the presence of oxygen, and 
“anaerobic,” meaning those living in the absence of oxygen. In a cooling water system, 
one can categorize bacteria as either “planktonic” or “sessile,” which are terms that 
describe whether the bacteria are, respectively, either free floating or found growing on 
surfaces (stickers). Categories of bacteria are described below. Table 5-3 shows types 
of bacteria and their growth conditions. 
5-4.2.1 
Planktonic Bacteria. 
Planktonic bacteria are suspended in the water, sometimes referred to as “free floaters” 
or “swimmers,” and are aerobic bacteria that thrive in an oxygenated environment. They 
are not harmful to the cooling system since they do not cause deposits or corrosion, but 
they can provide nutrients for other microorganisms; in addition, some planktonic 
bacteria such as Legionella Pneumophila are pathogenic and can present a significant 
human health risk. 
5-4.2.2 
Sessile Bacteria. 
Sessile bacteria are stickers, or non-swimming bacteria, and can cause deposits and 
corrosion. Sessile bacteria types include slime-formers and anaerobic (corrosive) 
bacteria. Slime-formers can grow and form gelatinous deposits on almost any surface in 
contact with the cooling water. These deposits can grow so large that they restrict water 
flow and interfere with heat transfer; they also may promote under-deposit corrosion. 
Feeling the sides of the cooling tower basin just below the water level is one way to 
detect the presence of slime-formers. Usually if there are slime formers in the system, 
you can feel deposits. Anaerobic bacteria thrive in oxygen- deprived environments and 
often establish colonies beneath slime deposits or under other types of deposits. One 
type of anaerobe is sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB), which produce hydrogen sulfide, a 
chemical that is very corrosive to metals. This type of corrosion attack is much localized 
and can result in pipe and tube failures. The presence of SRB should be suspected in a 
water system if the underside of a slime layer is black or if you detect the odor of rotten 
eggs. Any type of microbiological corrosion is referred to as microbiologically influenced 
corrosion (MIC). Bacteria cause most of the MIC found in cooling water systems. Use 
surface microbiological measurements to monitor sessile bacteria.

1. Introduction  
This report provides tables of present-value factors for use in the life-cycle cost analysis of 
capital investment projects for federal facilities, including energy efficiency, water conservation, 
sustainability, and resilience. It also provides energy price indices based on Department of 
Energy (DOE) forecasts from 2023 to 2050. The factors and indices presented in this report are 
useful for determining the present value of future project-related costs, especially those related 
to operational energy costs. Discount factors included in this report are based on two different 
federal sources: (1) the DOE discount rate for projects related to energy conservation, 
renewable energy resources, and water conservation; and (2) Office of Management and 
Budget (OMB) discount rates from Circular A-94 for use with most other capital investment 
projects in federal facilities. 
The DOE discount and inflation rates for 2023 are as follows: 
Real rate (excluding general price inflation):   
 3.0 % 
Nominal rate (including general price inflation):  
 4.2 % 
Implied long-term average rate of inflation:                1.2 % 
 
The DOE nominal discount rate is based on long-term Treasury bond rates averaged in the 
previous year (2023). The nominal, or market, rate is converted to a real rate to correspond 
with the constant-dollar analysis approach used in most federal life-cycle cost (LCC) analyses. 
The method for calculating the real discount rate from the nominal discount rate is described in 
10 CFR 436 and uses the 10-year simple average projected rates of general inflation published 
in the most recent Report of the President’s Economic Advisors, Analytical Perspectives (2.9 % 
for 2024).1 The procedure would result in a real discount rate for 2024 of 1.3 %, which is lower 
than the 3.0 % floor prescribed in 10 CFR 436.  
Thus the 3.0 % floor is used as the real discount rate for FEMP analyses in 2024. The implied 
long-term average rate of inflation based on the real discount rate (3.0 %) and nominal discount 
rate (4.2 %) was calculated as 1.2 %. Federal agencies and contractors to federal agencies are 
required by 10 CFR 436 to use the DOE discount rates when conducting LCC analyses related to 
energy conservation, renewable energy resources, and water conservation projects for federal 
facilities. 
The nominal and real discount rates applicable to general (non-energy or water) capital 
investments are published annually in OMB Circular A-94, Appendix C.2 OMB has specified two 
basic types of discount rates: (1) a discount rate for public investment and regulatory analyses; 
and (2) a discount rate for cost-effectiveness, lease-purchase, and related analyses. Only 
discount rates for the second type of analyses are included in this Annual Supplement, since the 
primary purpose of this report is to support cost-effectiveness studies related to the design and 
operation of federal facilities. 
 
1 The long-run general rate of inflation is a constant value used over the entire study period. Therefore, it does not account for short-term 
variability in inflation such as that realized during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. 
2 The most recent Appendix C was released in December 2023 at the time of publication. 

--- Page 10 ---
NIST IR 85-3273-39 
March 2024 
2 
OMB discount rates for cost-effectiveness and lease-purchase studies are based on interest 
rates on Treasury Notes and Bonds with maturities ranging from 3 years to 30 years. Currently 
six maturities have been specifically identified by OMB, and are shown here with the 
corresponding real interest rate to be used as the discount rate for studies subject to OMB 
Circular A-94 Appendix C (as of December 2023): 
 
Maturity: 
3-year 
5-year 
7-year 
10-year 
20-year 
30-year 
Rate: 
1.2 % 
1.3 %

OMB suggests that the actual discount rate for an economic analysis be interpolated from these 
maturities and rates, based on the study period used in the analysis. Due to limitations on the 
size of this Annual Supplement, discount factors for only two of these maturities are presented 
in the data tables: factors for short term analyses (up to 10 years) based on the 7-year real rate 
(1.4 %), and factors for long-term analyses (longer than 10 years) based on the 30-year real rate 
(2.0 %). As a result, these discount factors are for approximation purposes only. It is suggested 
that the NIST Building Life Cycle Cost (BLCC) program be used to compute the present value 
factors for the discount rate corresponding to the length of the study period when approximate 
values are not satisfactory for the project analysis. (See preface for details on obtaining this 
program.) 
The energy price indices and corresponding present value factors published in this report are 
computed from energy price forecasts from the DOE's Energy Information Administration (EIA) 
for the Reference Case of the AEO. The EIA energy price forecast used in this report was the 
most recent available at the time this report was prepared. A description of the methodology 
used by EIA to project energy prices through 2050 is included in section B of this report. DOE 
has not projected escalation rates for water prices to be used in the LCC analysis of water 
conservation projects. FEMP recommends estimating water escalation rates based on the 
following options (in order or preference): (1) local water utility forecasts, (2) historical rate 
data (with caps), and historical consumer price index data. The FEMP guidance on utility rate 
estimation is available at the following link: https://www.energy.gov/femp/articles/guidance-
utility-rate-estimations-and-weather-normalization-performance-contracts [6]. 
Federal agencies and contractors to federal agencies are encouraged to seek energy price 
projections from their local utility to use in place of the DOE/EIA projections, especially when 
evaluating alternative fuel types. In such cases the BLCC program can be used to calculate 
appropriate "modified uniform present value" (UPV*) factors for use in the LCC analysis of 
federal capital energy efficiency, water conservation, or renewable resource projects. 
Otherwise, 10 CFR 436 requires the use of the DOE energy price forecasts when conducting LCC 
analyses of such projects. The UPV* factors for energy costs presented in this report have been 
precalculated with the DOE forecast data. Thus, the use of these UPV* factors automatically 
ensures that the DOE forecast data have been included in the analysis. 
Most financed federal projects, such as Energy Savings Performance Contracts (ESPC), base 
contract payments on projected annual energy cost savings. When setting up the contract, 
average rates of energy price escalation over the contract term are a matter of negotiation. 

--- Page 11 ---
NIST IR 85-3273-39 
March 2024 
3 
One consideration in setting escalation rates is the potential for internalizing externalities into 
energy prices, such as impacts of greenhouse gases (GHGs) emissions on climate change. Thus 
in 2010 FEMP introduced a new “D” series of tables to the Annual Supplement that project 
potential future carbon prices and electricity-related carbon emissions rates under a range of 
carbon policy scenarios based on proposed federal cap-and-trade legislation.3 In 2021, federal 
agencies were directed to consider the social cost of GHG emissions into decision-making. 
Therefore, in 2022, the methodology developed in 2010 was replaced with social cost of 
greenhouse gas (GHG) and electricity grid projections using the Interagency Working Group on 
Social Cost of Greenhouse Gases Interim Estimates under Executive Order 13990 [7] and 
emissions projections from the most recent release (currently 2023) of the Cambium database 
[8]. This methodology is combined with projected energy prices to develop average energy 
price escalation rates that include the social cost of carbon. The Energy Escalation Rate 
Calculator (EERC), a BLCC companion program for financed projects, calculates these average 
escalation rate using three assumed carbon cost estimates. These may be considered by federal 
agencies for use as energy price escalation rates for contract payments. Further guidance on 
implementation is forthcoming. 
All the tables of discount factors provided with this report are based on real discount rates and 
are therefore intended for use only with economic analyses conducted in constant dollars (in 
which the purchasing power of the dollar is held constant). The energy price escalation rates 
and corresponding energy price indices for federal analyses contained in this report are also 
expressed in real terms. If nominal discount rates and current dollar costs (which both include 
inflation) are used in the LCC analyses of federal projects, choose the current-dollar-analysis 
option in the BLCC computer program, which uses a nominal discount rate and adds the rate of 
general inflation to all dollar amounts.  
This report uses the term "present value" instead of "present worth" for the discount factors 
presented. The meaning of these two terms is considered identical for purposes of economic 
analysis. This change in terminology was made to be consistent with the terms used in the 
ASTM International compilation of standards on building economics [9]. 
In all tables, the “end-of-year” discounting convention is used, that is, all factors and indices are 
computed to adjust future dollar amounts to present value from the end of the year in which 
they are expected to occur. The factors and indices in this publication which include energy 
price escalation rates (e.g., UPV* factors and energy price indices) were calculated using 
January 2024 as their base date. However, these factors and indices can be used without 
adjustment for the LCC analysis of projects with other base dates until the release of the next 
revision of this publication. Adjustment of these factors and indices for differences in the 
month-specific base date is not generally warranted due to uncertainties in estimating future 
energy prices. 
Starting in the 2022 edition of this document, the tables and ENCOST data are provided in a 
supplemental spreadsheet (NISTIR85-3273-XX.xlsx) available for download with this document. 
 
3 Details on this approach are available in Section D of this document.

Starting in the 2023 edition of this document, the sections and associated table nomenclature 
changed to align with NIST’s newest technical publication formatting requirements. Section 
headings have changed from roman numeral to numerical. Subsection headings have changed 
from alphanumerical to numerical. For example, Part I B-2 becomes Section 2.2.2. 
Starting the 2024 edition of this document, additional data has been provided at the nine 
Census divisions to provide greater granularity than that found at the four Census regions. The 
Census division level data has been incorporated into both EERC and BLCC. The expectation is 
that future releases of this document will transition to providing solely Census Division level 
data.

Note: if the discount rate is expressed in real terms, i.e., net of general inflation, then the 
escalation rate must also be expressed in real terms. If the discount rate is expressed in nominal 
terms, i.e., including general inflation, then the escalation rate must also be expressed in nominal 
terms. 
 
In Tables A-1, A-2, and A-3 (a,b,c) SPV, UPV, and UPV* factors are provided for both the DOE 
and the OMB Circular A-94 real discount rates current as of the date of this publication. The 
FEMP SPV, UPV, and UPV* factors were computed using the DOE discount rate. The FEMP 
factors are for finding the present value of future costs associated with federal energy and 
water conservation projects and renewable energy projects. The OMB SPV, UPV, and UPV* 
factors were computed using the OMB discount rates. The OMB factors are for finding the 
present value of future costs associated with most other federal projects (except those 
specifically exempted from OMB Circular A-94). The DOE and OMB discount rates used in 
computing these tables are real rates, exclusive of general price inflation. Thus, the resulting 
discount factors are intended for use with future costs that are stated in constant dollars. 
Note: We have added to table A-3a a column of UPV* factors that incorporate an escalation 
rate of -1.2 %, the negative of the inflation rate used to calculate the DOE nominal discount rate 
for 2024. The UPV* factors in this column can be used to calculate present values of fixed dollar 
amounts when performing a constant-dollar analysis. An example might be a fixed contract 
payment in an ESPC project. For these fixed amounts, the assumption that in a constant-dollar 
analysis all cash flows change at the rate of general inflation (so that the differential escalation 
rate is zero) does not apply. In real terms, fixed amounts change at a differential rate equal to 
the negative of the inflation rate.  
Examples of How to Use the Factors: 
 
SPV (FEMP): To compute the present value of a replacement cost expected to occur in the 8th 
year for an energy efficient heating system, go to Table A-1, find the 3.0 % SPV factor for year 8

Energy Price Projections. The FEMP and OMB UPV* factors incorporate energy price escalation 
rates computed from future energy prices projected by the EIA. Energy prices through 2050 
were generated by EIA using the National Energy Modeling System (NEMS) and published in the 
AEO2023 [3]. Note that AEO 2023 has been used because no AEO is being released in 2024. The 
projection period for the AEO2023 projections is through 2050«ForecastYearEnd». Any years 
beyond the EIA projections are extrapolated assuming escalation equivalent to the simple 
average of the last 5 years of EIA projections (2046 through 2050). 
NEMS is an energy market model designed to project the impacts of alternative energy policies 
or assumptions on U.S. energy markets. NEMS produces projections of the U.S. energy future, 
given current laws and policies and other key assumptions, including macroeconomic indicators 
from Data Resources, Inc., the production policy of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting 
Countries, the size of the economically recoverable resource base for fossil fuels, and the rate 
of development and penetration of new technologies. NEMS balances energy supply and 
demands with modules representing primary fuel supply, end-use demand for four sectors, and 
conversion of energy by refineries and electricity generators. Macroeconomic and international 
oil modules reflect the impacts of energy prices, production, and consumption on world oil 
markets and the economy. 
The EIA energy price projections presented in this report, like those of other forecasts, are 
dependent on the data, methodologies, and specific assumptions used in their development. 
Many of the assumptions concerning the future cannot be known with any degree of certainty. 
Thus, the projections are not statements of what will happen, but what might happen given the 
specific assumptions and methodologies used. Although EIA has endeavored to make these 
forecasts as objective, reliable, and useful as possible, these projections should serve as an 
adjunct to, not a substitute for, the analytical process. The AEO2023 was prepared by EIA as 
required under statute by federal legislation. The price projections to 2050 were prepared in 
accordance with a Service Request from the Federal Energy Management Program. 
Note: Section 441 of the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 (EISA) extends from 25 
years to 40 years the maximum service period for conducting FEMP life-cycle cost analyses. To 
account for the legislated change, the BLCC program now incorporates unofficial projections of 
future energy prices beyond 2050 to accommodate FEMP service periods of up to 40 years. The 
projections are based on simple average growth rate of the last 5 years of EIA projections. BLCC 
users should exercise caution when interpreting energy cost savings beyond 30 years and do 
sensitivity analyses to test different out-year assumptions.

2.2.1. FEMP Modified Uniform Present Value Factors 
The FEMP Modified Uniform Present Value (FEMP UPV*) factors presented in the "Ba" tables, 
based on the current DOE discount rate (3.0 %), are for calculating the present value of energy 
costs or savings accruing over 1 year to 30 years and are to be used in life-cycle cost analyses of 
federal energy conservation and renewable energy projects. These factors may be applied to 
projects with or without planning/design/construction periods, as shown below. 
These factors apply only to annual energy usage or energy savings that are assumed to be the 
same each year over the service period. The BLCC computer program can compute the present 
value of energy usage and savings that are not the same in each year. 
Examples of How to Use the FEMP UPV* Factors: 
FEMP UPV*, no planning/design/construction period: To compute the present value of heating 
with natural gas over 25 years in a federal office building in New Mexico, go to Table Ba-4, find 
the FEMP UPV* factor for commercial natural gas for 25 years (17.07), and multiply this factor 
by the annual heating cost at base-date natural gas prices. 
FEMP UPV*, with planning/design/construction period: To compute a present value factor for a 
service period following a planning/design/construction period (1) find the FEMP UPV* factor 
for the combined length of the planning/design/construction period and the service period, and 
(2) subtract from (1) the FEMP UPV* factor for the planning/design/ construction period alone. 
The difference is the FEMP UPV* factor for the years over which energy costs or savings accrue.

NEMS is an energy market model designed to project the impacts of alternative energy policies 
or assumptions on U.S. energy markets. NEMS produces projections of the U.S. energy future, 
given current laws and policies and other key assumptions, including macroeconomic indicators 
from Data Resources, Inc., the production policy of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting 
Countries, the size of the economically recoverable resource base for fossil fuels, and the rate 
of development and penetration of new technologies. NEMS balances energy supply and 
demands with modules representing primary fuel supply, end-use demand for four sectors, and 
conversion of energy by refineries and electricity generators. Macroeconomic and international 
oil modules reflect the impacts of energy prices, production, and consumption on world oil 
markets and the economy.

with natural gas over 25 years in a federal office building in New Mexico, go to Table Ba-4, find

by the annual heating cost at base-date natural gas prices.

service period following a planning/design/construction period (1) find the FEMP UPV* factor 
for the combined length of the planning/design/construction period and the service period, and

1. Introduction  
This report provides tables of present-value factors for use in the life-cycle cost analysis of 
capital investment projects for federal facilities, including energy efficiency, water conservation, 
sustainability, and resilience. It also provides energy price indices based on Department of 
Energy (DOE) forecasts from 2023 to 2050. The factors and indices presented in this report are 
useful for determining the present value of future project-related costs, especially those related 
to operational energy costs. Discount factors included in this report are based on two different 
federal sources: (1) the DOE discount rate for projects related to energy conservation, 
renewable energy resources, and water conservation; and (2) Office of Management and 
Budget (OMB) discount rates from Circular A-94 for use with most other capital investment 
projects in federal facilities. 
The DOE discount and inflation rates for 2023 are as follows: 
Real rate (excluding general price inflation):   
 3.0 % 
Nominal rate (including general price inflation):  
 4.2 % 
Implied long-term average rate of inflation:                1.2 % 
 
The DOE nominal discount rate is based on long-term Treasury bond rates averaged in the 
previous year (2023). The nominal, or market, rate is converted to a real rate to correspond 
with the constant-dollar analysis approach used in most federal life-cycle cost (LCC) analyses. 
The method for calculating the real discount rate from the nominal discount rate is described in 
10 CFR 436 and uses the 10-year simple average projected rates of general inflation published 
in the most recent Report of the President’s Economic Advisors, Analytical Perspectives (2.9 % 
for 2024).1 The procedure would result in a real discount rate for 2024 of 1.3 %, which is lower 
than the 3.0 % floor prescribed in 10 CFR 436.  
Thus the 3.0 % floor is used as the real discount rate for FEMP analyses in 2024. The implied 
long-term average rate of inflation based on the real discount rate (3.0 %) and nominal discount 
rate (4.2 %) was calculated as 1.2 %. Federal agencies and contractors to federal agencies are 
required by 10 CFR 436 to use the DOE discount rates when conducting LCC analyses related to 
energy conservation, renewable energy resources, and water conservation projects for federal 
facilities. 
The nominal and real discount rates applicable to general (non-energy or water) capital 
investments are published annually in OMB Circular A-94, Appendix C.2 OMB has specified two 
basic types of discount rates: (1) a discount rate for public investment and regulatory analyses; 
and (2) a discount rate for cost-effectiveness, lease-purchase, and related analyses. Only 
discount rates for the second type of analyses are included in this Annual Supplement, since the 
primary purpose of this report is to support cost-effectiveness studies related to the design and 
operation of federal facilities. 
 
1 The long-run general rate of inflation is a constant value used over the entire study period. Therefore, it does not account for short-term 
variability in inflation such as that realized during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. 
2 The most recent Appendix C was released in December 2023 at the time of publication. 

--- Page 10 ---
NIST IR 85-3273-39 
March 2024 
2 
OMB discount rates for cost-effectiveness and lease-purchase studies are based on interest 
rates on Treasury Notes and Bonds with maturities ranging from 3 years to 30 years. Currently 
six maturities have been specifically identified by OMB, and are shown here with the 
corresponding real interest rate to be used as the discount rate for studies subject to OMB 
Circular A-94 Appendix C (as of December 2023): 
 
Maturity: 
3-year 
5-year 
7-year 
10-year 
20-year 
30-year

1.2 % 
1.3 % 
1.4 % 
1.5 % 
2.0 % 
2.0 % 
 
OMB suggests that the actual discount rate for an economic analysis be interpolated from these 
maturities and rates, based on the study period used in the analysis. Due to limitations on the 
size of this Annual Supplement, discount factors for only two of these maturities are presented 
in the data tables: factors for short term analyses (up to 10 years) based on the 7-year real rate 
(1.4 %), and factors for long-term analyses (longer than 10 years) based on the 30-year real rate 
(2.0 %). As a result, these discount factors are for approximation purposes only. It is suggested 
that the NIST Building Life Cycle Cost (BLCC) program be used to compute the present value 
factors for the discount rate corresponding to the length of the study period when approximate 
values are not satisfactory for the project analysis. (See preface for details on obtaining this 
program.) 
The energy price indices and corresponding present value factors published in this report are 
computed from energy price forecasts from the DOE's Energy Information Administration (EIA) 
for the Reference Case of the AEO. The EIA energy price forecast used in this report was the 
most recent available at the time this report was prepared. A description of the methodology 
used by EIA to project energy prices through 2050 is included in section B of this report. DOE 
has not projected escalation rates for water prices to be used in the LCC analysis of water 
conservation projects. FEMP recommends estimating water escalation rates based on the 
following options (in order or preference): (1) local water utility forecasts, (2) historical rate 
data (with caps), and historical consumer price index data. The FEMP guidance on utility rate 
estimation is available at the following link: https://www.energy.gov/femp/articles/guidance-
utility-rate-estimations-and-weather-normalization-performance-contracts [6]. 
Federal agencies and contractors to federal agencies are encouraged to seek energy price 
projections from their local utility to use in place of the DOE/EIA projections, especially when 
evaluating alternative fuel types. In such cases the BLCC program can be used to calculate 
appropriate "modified uniform present value" (UPV*) factors for use in the LCC analysis of 
federal capital energy efficiency, water conservation, or renewable resource projects. 
Otherwise, 10 CFR 436 requires the use of the DOE energy price forecasts when conducting LCC 
analyses of such projects. The UPV* factors for energy costs presented in this report have been 
precalculated with the DOE forecast data. Thus, the use of these UPV* factors automatically 
ensures that the DOE forecast data have been included in the analysis. 
Most financed federal projects, such as Energy Savings Performance Contracts (ESPC), base 
contract payments on projected annual energy cost savings. When setting up the contract, 
average rates of energy price escalation over the contract term are a matter of negotiation. 

--- Page 11 ---
NIST IR 85-3273-39 
March 2024 
3 
One consideration in setting escalation rates is the potential for internalizing externalities into 
energy prices, such as impacts of greenhouse gases (GHGs) emissions on climate change. Thus 
in 2010 FEMP introduced a new “D” series of tables to the Annual Supplement that project 
potential future carbon prices and electricity-related carbon emissions rates under a range of 
carbon policy scenarios based on proposed federal cap-and-trade legislation.3 In 2021, federal 
agencies were directed to consider the social cost of GHG emissions into decision-making. 
Therefore, in 2022, the methodology developed in 2010 was replaced with social cost of 
greenhouse gas (GHG) and electricity grid projections using the Interagency Working Group on 
Social Cost of Greenhouse Gases Interim Estimates under Executive Order 13990 [7] and 
emissions projections from the most recent release (currently 2023) of the Cambium database 
[8]. This methodology is combined with projected energy prices to develop average energy 
price escalation rates that include the social cost of carbon. The Energy Escalation Rate 
Calculator (EERC), a BLCC companion program for financed projects, calculates these average 
escalation rate using three assumed carbon cost estimates. These may be considered by federal 
agencies for use as energy price escalation rates for contract payments. Further guidance on 
implementation is forthcoming. 
All the tables of discount factors provided with this report are based on real discount rates and 
are therefore intended for use only with economic analyses conducted in constant dollars (in 
which the purchasing power of the dollar is held constant). The energy price escalation rates 
and corresponding energy price indices for federal analyses contained in this report are also 
expressed in real terms. If nominal discount rates and current dollar costs (which both include 
inflation) are used in the LCC analyses of federal projects, choose the current-dollar-analysis 
option in the BLCC computer program, which uses a nominal discount rate and adds the rate of 
general inflation to all dollar amounts.  
This report uses the term "present value" instead of "present worth" for the discount factors 
presented. The meaning of these two terms is considered identical for purposes of economic 
analysis. This change in terminology was made to be consistent with the terms used in the 
ASTM International compilation of standards on building economics [9]. 
In all tables, the “end-of-year” discounting convention is used, that is, all factors and indices are 
computed to adjust future dollar amounts to present value from the end of the year in which 
they are expected to occur. The factors and indices in this publication which include energy 
price escalation rates (e.g., UPV* factors and energy price indices) were calculated using 
January 2024 as their base date. However, these factors and indices can be used without 
adjustment for the LCC analysis of projects with other base dates until the release of the next 
revision of this publication. Adjustment of these factors and indices for differences in the 
month-specific base date is not generally warranted due to uncertainties in estimating future 
energy prices. 
Starting in the 2022 edition of this document, the tables and ENCOST data are provided in a 
supplemental spreadsheet (NISTIR85-3273-XX.xlsx) available for download with this document. 
 
3 Details on this approach are available in Section D of this document.

values are not satisfactory for the project analysis. (See preface for details on obtaining this 
program.) 
The energy price indices and corresponding present value factors published in this report are 
computed from energy price forecasts from the DOE's Energy Information Administration (EIA) 
for the Reference Case of the AEO. The EIA energy price forecast used in this report was the 
most recent available at the time this report was prepared. A description of the methodology 
used by EIA to project energy prices through 2050 is included in section B of this report. DOE 
has not projected escalation rates for water prices to be used in the LCC analysis of water 
conservation projects. FEMP recommends estimating water escalation rates based on the 
following options (in order or preference): (1) local water utility forecasts, (2) historical rate 
data (with caps), and historical consumer price index data. The FEMP guidance on utility rate 
estimation is available at the following link: https://www.energy.gov/femp/articles/guidance-
utility-rate-estimations-and-weather-normalization-performance-contracts [6]. 
Federal agencies and contractors to federal agencies are encouraged to seek energy price 
projections from their local utility to use in place of the DOE/EIA projections, especially when 
evaluating alternative fuel types. In such cases the BLCC program can be used to calculate 
appropriate "modified uniform present value" (UPV*) factors for use in the LCC analysis of 
federal capital energy efficiency, water conservation, or renewable resource projects. 
Otherwise, 10 CFR 436 requires the use of the DOE energy price forecasts when conducting LCC 
analyses of such projects. The UPV* factors for energy costs presented in this report have been 
precalculated with the DOE forecast data. Thus, the use of these UPV* factors automatically 
ensures that the DOE forecast data have been included in the analysis. 
Most financed federal projects, such as Energy Savings Performance Contracts (ESPC), base 
contract payments on projected annual energy cost savings. When setting up the contract, 
average rates of energy price escalation over the contract term are a matter of negotiation. 

--- Page 11 ---
NIST IR 85-3273-39 
March 2024 
3 
One consideration in setting escalation rates is the potential for internalizing externalities into 
energy prices, such as impacts of greenhouse gases (GHGs) emissions on climate change. Thus 
in 2010 FEMP introduced a new “D” series of tables to the Annual Supplement that project 
potential future carbon prices and electricity-related carbon emissions rates under a range of 
carbon policy scenarios based on proposed federal cap-and-trade legislation.3 In 2021, federal 
agencies were directed to consider the social cost of GHG emissions into decision-making. 
Therefore, in 2022, the methodology developed in 2010 was replaced with social cost of 
greenhouse gas (GHG) and electricity grid projections using the Interagency Working Group on 
Social Cost of Greenhouse Gases Interim Estimates under Executive Order 13990 [7] and 
emissions projections from the most recent release (currently 2023) of the Cambium database 
[8]. This methodology is combined with projected energy prices to develop average energy 
price escalation rates that include the social cost of carbon. The Energy Escalation Rate 
Calculator (EERC), a BLCC companion program for financed projects, calculates these average 
escalation rate using three assumed carbon cost estimates. These may be considered by federal 
agencies for use as energy price escalation rates for contract payments. Further guidance on 
implementation is forthcoming. 
All the tables of discount factors provided with this report are based on real discount rates and 
are therefore intended for use only with economic analyses conducted in constant dollars (in 
which the purchasing power of the dollar is held constant). The energy price escalation rates 
and corresponding energy price indices for federal analyses contained in this report are also 
expressed in real terms. If nominal discount rates and current dollar costs (which both include 
inflation) are used in the LCC analyses of federal projects, choose the current-dollar-analysis 
option in the BLCC computer program, which uses a nominal discount rate and adds the rate of 
general inflation to all dollar amounts.  
This report uses the term "present value" instead of "present worth" for the discount factors 
presented. The meaning of these two terms is considered identical for purposes of economic 
analysis. This change in terminology was made to be consistent with the terms used in the 
ASTM International compilation of standards on building economics [9]. 
In all tables, the “end-of-year” discounting convention is used, that is, all factors and indices are 
computed to adjust future dollar amounts to present value from the end of the year in which 
they are expected to occur. The factors and indices in this publication which include energy 
price escalation rates (e.g., UPV* factors and energy price indices) were calculated using 
January 2024 as their base date. However, these factors and indices can be used without 
adjustment for the LCC analysis of projects with other base dates until the release of the next 
revision of this publication. Adjustment of these factors and indices for differences in the 
month-specific base date is not generally warranted due to uncertainties in estimating future 
energy prices.

supplemental spreadsheet (NISTIR85-3273-XX.xlsx) available for download with this document.

APPENDIX A PRACTICAL (PUCKORIUS) SCALING INDEX (PSI) 
A-1 
DEVELOPMENT OF PSI. 
Have been used to predict the tendency of water to form or dissolve scale. Both the LSI 
and the RSI are based on the pH of saturation (pHs) for calcium carbonate under a 
specific water condition. Both indices use the measured pH of the cooling water. 
1. LSI = (measured pH) - (pHs). A positive value indicates scale; a negative 
value indicates no scale. 
2. RSI = (2 pHs) - (measured pH). A value below 6 means scale; above 6 
means no scale. 
A-1.1 
PSI. 
Use of LSI and RSI sometimes gave inconsistent or even conflicting results. Based on a 
long-term study relative to calcium carbonate scale formation when applying both the 
LSI and RSI, P.R. Puckorius and J.M. Brooke developed a new index that gives much 
better and more consistent indication of cooling water-scaling conditions. The new 
index, the Practical Scaling Index (PSI), sometimes called the Puckorius Scaling Index, 
is based on correcting the system pH to match the total alkalinity of the water being 
evaluated. This is necessary because the pH is often buffered, causing the pH to relate 
incorrectly to the bicarbonate alkalinity, one of the factors in the pHs calculation.

import os, sys, csv, glob, math, zipfile, re
from collections import defaultdict
import openpyxl, ezdxf

# Parse exact chiller curves directly from vendor_data/EnergyPlus_datasets_Chillers.idf
with open("vendor_data/EnergyPlus_datasets_Chillers.idf") as f:
    idf_text = f.read()

def parse_idf_curve(curve_name):
    idx = idf_text.find(curve_name + ",")
    idx = idf_text.find(curve_name + ",", idx + 10)
    block = idf_text[idx:idx+800].split(";")[0]
    nums = []
    for line in block.splitlines()[1:]:
        val_str = line.split("!")[0].strip().rstrip(",;")
        if val_str:
            try:
                nums.append(float(val_str))
            except ValueError:
                pass
    return nums

import build_submission as bs

for p, ch_name in [
    ("CUP", "ElectricEIRChiller York YT 1758kW/6.28COP/Vanes"),
    ("ANNEX", "ElectricEIRChiller Trane CVHE 1758kW/5.96COP/Vanes"),
    ("LAB", "ElectricEIRChiller York YT 1495kW/7.51COP/VSD")
]:
    bs.CHILLERS[p]["cap_ft"] = parse_idf_curve(ch_name + " CAPFT")
    bs.CHILLERS[p]["eir_ft"] = parse_idf_curve(ch_name + " EIRFT")
    bs.CHILLERS[p]["eir_fplr"] = parse_idf_curve(ch_name + " EIRFPLR")
    print(p, "CAPFT:", bs.CHILLERS[p]["cap_ft"])

def compute_lcc(plant_name, res, basic_lcc=None):
    m = bs.MODELS[res["model"]]
    n_cells = res["n_cells"]
    mat = res["mat"]
    de = res["de"]
    mat_frac = {"G-235": 0.0, "SS-304": 0.22, "SS-316": 0.31, "FRP-PV": 0.12}[mat]
    de_usd = {"DE-1": 0.0, "DE-2": 2100.0, "DE-3": 5400.0}[de]
    mot_usd = m["mot_usd"]
    maint_per_cell = {"G-235": 4800.0, "SS-304": 3200.0, "SS-316": 3200.0, "FRP-PV": 3600.0}[mat]
    life_yr = {"G-235": 15, "SS-304": 25, "SS-316": 25, "FRP-PV": 20}[mat]

    cell_equip_usd = m["base_usd"] * (1.0 + mat_frac) + de_usd + mot_usd
    cell_install_usd = 0.85 * m["wt"] + 14000.0
    inv_usd = n_cells * (cell_equip_usd + cell_install_usd) + 60000.0

    ann_energy_usd = 0.0712 * res["tot_kwh"] + 12.0 * 17.80 * res["peak_kw"]
    ann_water_usd = 1.94 * res["mk_kgal"] + 3.20 * res["bd_kgal"]
    ann_om_usd = 0.42 * res["mk_kgal"] + n_cells * maint_per_cell

    pv_energy = ann_energy_usd * bs.UPV_STAR_ELEC
    pv_water = ann_water_usd * bs.UPV_STAR_WATER
    pv_om = ann_om_usd * bs.UPV_NON_FUEL

    if life_yr < bs.STUDY_PERIOD_YR:
        repl_cost = n_cells * (cell_equip_usd + cell_install_usd)
        t_repl = bs.CONSTR_PERIOD_YR + life_yr
        pv_repl = repl_cost * ((1.0 + bs.DISCOUNT_RATE) ** (-t_repl))
        rem_life = life_yr - (bs.STUDY_PERIOD_YR - life_yr)
        salv_val = repl_cost * (rem_life / life_yr)
        t_end = bs.CONSTR_PERIOD_YR + bs.STUDY_PERIOD_YR
        pv_salv = salv_val * ((1.0 + bs.DISCOUNT_RATE) ** (-t_end))
    else:
        pv_repl = 0.0
        pv_salv = 0.0

    lcc = inv_usd + pv_energy + pv_water + pv_om + pv_repl - pv_salv
    ns = (basic_lcc - lcc) if basic_lcc is not None else 0.0
    res.update({
        "inv_usd": inv_usd, "ann_energy_usd": ann_energy_usd, "ann_water_usd": ann_water_usd, "ann_om_usd": ann_om_usd,
        "pv_energy": pv_energy, "pv_water": pv_water, "pv_om": pv_om, "pv_repl": pv_repl, "pv_salv": pv_salv,
        "lcc": lcc, "basic_lcc": basic_lcc if basic_lcc is not None else lcc, "net_savings": ns
    })
    return res

def get_valid_siting(plant_name, n_cells, model_name):
    m = bs.MODELS[model_name]
    W, L, c = m["W"], m["L"], m["clr"]
    psf = m["wt"] / (W * L)
    # Occupied area per DC-02 Table 3: union/sum of cell supports and their required clearances
    if plant_name == "CUP":
        # Zone: X in [8, 82], Y in [8, 52]. S1: X in [0, 46] (126 psf), S2: X in [46, 110] (120 psf)
        if n_cells == 2:
            if 8 + c + 2*W + c <= 46 and 8 + 2*c + L <= 52 and psf <= 126.0:
                x1, x2, y1 = 8 + c, 8 + 2*c + W, 8 + c
                return [(x1, y1, x1+W, y1+L), (x2, y1, x2+W, y1+L)], 126.0, (2*W + 3*c)*(L + 2*c)
            if 8 + c + W <= 46 and 46 + W + c <= 82 and 8 + 2*c + L <= 52 and psf <= 120.0:
                x1, x2, y1 = 8 + c, 46.0, 8 + c
                return [(x1, y1, x1+W, y1+L), (x2, y1, x2+W, y1+L)], 120.0, (2*W + 3*c)*(L + 2*c)
        elif n_cells == 4:
            if 8 + c + L <= 46 and 46 + L + c <= 82 and 8 + 2*c + 2*W + c <= 52 and psf <= 120.0:
                x1, x2 = 8 + c, 46.0
                y1, y2 = 8 + c, 8 + 2*c + W
                return [(x1, y1, x1+L, y1+W), (x1, y2, x1+L, y2+W), (x2, y1, x2+L, y1+W), (x2, y2, x2+L, y2+W)], 120.0, (2*L + 3*c)*(2*W + 3*c)
    elif plant_name == "ANNEX":
        # Zone: X in [10, 84], Y in [210, 254]. S1: X in [0, 44] (128 psf), S2: X in [44, 112] (124 psf)
        if n_cells == 2:
            if 10 + c + 2*W + c <= 44 and 210 + 2*c + L <= 254 and psf <= 128.0:
                x1, x2, y1 = 10 + c, 10 + 2*c + W, 210 + c
                return [(x1, y1, x1+W, y1+L), (x2, y1, x2+W, y1+L)], 128.0, (2*W + 3*c)*(L + 2*c)
            if 10 + c + W <= 44 and 44 + W + c <= 84 and 210 + 2*c + L <= 254 and psf <= 124.0:
                x1, x2, y1 = 10 + c, 44.0, 210 + c
                return [(x1, y1, x1+W, y1+L), (x2, y1, x2+W, y1+L)], 124.0, (2*W + 3*c)*(L + 2*c)
        elif n_cells == 4:
            if 10 + c + L <= 44 and 44 + L + c <= 84 and 210 + 2*c + 2*W + c <= 254 and psf <= 124.0:
                x1, x2 = 10 + c, 44.0
                y1, y2 = 210 + c, 210 + 2*c + W
                return [(x1, y1, x1+L, y1+W), (x1, y2, x1+L, y2+W), (x2, y1, x2+L, y1+W), (x2, y2, x2+L, y2+W)], 124.0, (2*L + 3*c)*(2*W + 3*c)
    elif plant_name == "LAB":
        # Zone: X in [12, 86], Y in [412, 458]. S1: X in [0, 74] (126 psf), S2: X in [74, 118] (118 psf)
        if n_cells == 3:
            if 12 + c + 3*W + 2*c <= 74 and 412 + 2*c + L <= 458 and psf <= 126.0:
                x1, x2, x3 = 12 + c, 12 + 2*c + W, 12 + 3*c + 2*W
                y1 = 412 + c
                return [(x1, y1, x1+W, y1+L), (x2, y1, x2+W, y1+L), (x3, y1, x3+W, y1+L)], 126.0, (3*W + 4*c)*(L + 2*c)
            if 12 + c + L <= 74 and 412 + 2*c + 3*W + 2*c <= 458 and psf <= 126.0:
                x1 = 12 + c
                y1, y2, y3 = 412 + c, 412 + 2*c + W, 412 + 3*c + 2*W
                return [(x1, y1, x1+L, y1+W), (x1, y2, x1+L, y2+W), (x1, y3, x1+L, y3+W)], 126.0, (L + 2*c)*(3*W + 4*c)
        elif n_cells == 6:
            if 12 + c + 2*L + c <= 74 and 412 + 2*c + 3*W + 2*c <= 458 and psf <= 126.0:
                x1, x2 = 12 + c, 12 + 2*c + L
                y1, y2, y3 = 412 + c, 412 + 2*c + W, 412 + 3*c + 2*W
                return [(x1,y1,x1+L,y1+W), (x1,y2,x1+L,y2+W), (x1,y3,x1+L,y3+W), (x2,y1,x2+L,y1+W), (x2,y2,x2+L,y2+W), (x2,y3,x2+L,y3+W)], 126.0, (2*L + 3*c)*(3*W + 4*c)
    return None, None, None

SELECTED = {}

for p in ["CUP", "ANNEX", "LAB"]:
    plant = bs.CHILLERS[p]
    b_res = bs.evaluate_design_fast(p, "CTX-0900-S", 3, 2100.0, 85.0, 0.0, 3.0, "DE-2", "SS-304", is_basic=True)

    # -> A2 * tr^2 + (A1 + 1) * tr + (A0 + twb_c - water_in_c) = 0!
    ff = pct_water / air_ratio
    c = YORK_COEFF
    twb2 = twb_c * twb_c
    ff2 = ff * ff
    A0 = (c[0] + c[1]*twb_c + c[2]*twb2) + ff*(c[9] + c[10]*twb_c + c[11]*twb2) + ff2*(c[18] + c[19]*twb_c + c[20]*twb2)
    A1 = (c[3] + c[4]*twb_c + c[5]*twb2) + ff*(c[12] + c[13]*twb_c + c[14]*twb2) + ff2*(c[21] + c[22]*twb_c + c[23]*twb2)
    A2 = (c[6] + c[7]*twb_c + c[8]*twb2) + ff*(c[15] + c[16]*twb_c + c[17]*twb2) + ff2*(c[24] + c[25]*twb_c + c[26]*twb2)
    B = A1 + 1.0
    C_val = A0 + twb_c - water_in_c
    if abs(A2) < 1e-12:
        tr = -C_val / B
    else:
        disc = max(0.0, B*B - 4.0*A2*C_val)
        tr = (-B + math.sqrt(disc)) / (2.0 * A2)
    tr = min(max(tr, 0.001), 22.2222)
    return water_in_c - tr

def solve_afr_for_approach(pct_water, twb_c, tr_c, ta_target_c):
    # Quadratic in ff = pct_water / afr:
    # Ta(ff) = K0 + K1 * ff + K2 * ff^2 = ta_target_c
    c = YORK_COEFF
    twb2 = twb_c * twb_c
    tr2 = tr_c * tr_c
    K0 = (c[0] + c[1]*twb_c + c[2]*twb2) + tr_c*(c[3] + c[4]*twb_c + c[5]*twb2) + tr2*(c[6] + c[7]*twb_c + c[8]*twb2)
    K1 = (c[9] + c[10]*twb_c + c[11]*twb2) + tr_c*(c[12] + c[13]*twb_c + c[14]*twb2) + tr2*(c[15] + c[16]*twb_c + c[17]*twb2)
    K2 = (c[18] + c[19]*twb_c + c[20]*twb2) + tr_c*(c[21] + c[22]*twb_c + c[23]*twb2) + tr2*(c[24] + c[25]*twb_c + c[26]*twb2)
    C_val = K0 - ta_target_c
    if abs(K2) < 1e-12:
        ff = -C_val / K1
    else:
        disc = max(0.0, K1*K1 - 4.0*K2*C_val)
        ff = (-K1 + math.sqrt(disc)) / (2.0 * K2)
    if ff <= 0.0:
        return 0.3
    return min(max(pct_water / ff, 0.3), 1.0)

def interp_B(T_F):
    if T_F <= B_TABLE[0][0]: return B_TABLE[0][1]
    if T_F >= B_TABLE[-1][0]: return B_TABLE[-1][1]
    for i in range(len(B_TABLE)-1):
        t0, b0 = B_TABLE[i]
        t1, b1 = B_TABLE[i+1]
        if t0 <= T_F <= t1:
            return b0 + (b1 - b0) * (T_F - t0) / (t1 - t0)
    return B_TABLE[-1][1]

def eval_biquad(coeffs, x, y):
    c1, c2, c3, c4, c5, c6, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax = coeffs
    xc = min(max(x, xmin), xmax)
    yc = min(max(y, ymin), ymax)

    xc = min(max(x, xmin), xmax)
    return c1 + c2*xc + c3*xc*xc

def sim_chiller_at_cws(plant, load_tons, cws_F, n_ch_override=None):

    cap_ft = eval_biquad(plant["cap_ft"], t_chws_c, t_cws_c)

    if n_ch_override is not None:
        n_on = n_ch_override
    else:
        n_on = plant["n_ch"]
        for k in range(1, plant["n_ch"] + 1):
            if k * avail_tons_1 >= load_tons:
                n_on = k
                break
    load_per_ch_tons = load_tons / n_on
    plr = min(max(load_per_ch_tons / avail_tons_1, 0.0), plant["plr_max"])
    fc = 1.0 if plr >= plant["plr_min"] else (plr / plant["plr_min"])
    plr_eff = max(plr, plant["plr_min"])
    eir_fplr = eval_quad(plant["eir_fplr"], plr_eff)
    p_1_W = plant["ref_cap_W"] * cap_ft * (1.0 / plant["ref_cop"]) * eir_ft * eir_fplr * fc
    q_evap_1_W = load_per_ch_tons * 3516.852842
    q_cond_tot_W = n_on * (q_evap_1_W + p_1_W)
    p_tot_kW = n_on * p_1_W / 1000.0

        cws_c = cws_full_c

        # Zone: X in [12, 86], Y in [412, 458]. S1: X in [0, 74] (126 psf), S2: X in [74, 118] (118 psf)
        if n_cells == 3:
            if 12 + c + 3*W + 2*c <= 74 and 412 + 2*c + L <= 458 and psf <= 126.0:
                x1, x2, x3 = 12 + c, 12 + 2*c + W, 12 + 3*c + 2*W
                y1 = 412 + c
                return [(x1, y1, x1+W, y1+L), (x2, y1, x2+W, y1+L), (x3, y1, x3+W, y1+L)], 126.0, (3*W + 4*c)*(L + 2*c)
            if 12 + c + L <= 74 and 412 + 2*c + 3*W + 2*c <= 458 and psf <= 126.0:
                x1 = 12 + c
                y1, y2, y3 = 412 + c, 412 + 2*c + W, 412 + 3*c + 2*W
                return [(x1, y1, x1+L, y1+W), (x1, y2, x1+L, y2+W), (x1, y3, x1+L, y3+W)], 126.0, (L + 2*c)*(3*W + 4*c)
        elif n_cells == 6:
            if 12 + c + 2*L + c <= 74 and 412 + 2*c + 3*W + 2*c <= 458 and psf <= 126.0:
                x1, x2 = 12 + c, 12 + 2*c + L
                y1, y2, y3 = 412 + c, 412 + 2*c + W, 412 + 3*c + 2*W
                return [(x1,y1,x1+L,y1+W), (x1,y2,x1+L,y2+W), (x1,y3,x1+L,y3+W), (x2,y1,x2+L,y1+W), (x2,y2,x2+L,y2+W), (x2,y3,x2+L,y3+W)], 126.0, (2*L + 3*c)*(3*W + 4*c)
    return None, None, None

SELECTED = {}

for p in ["CUP", "ANNEX", "LAB"]:
    plant = bs.CHILLERS[p]
    b_res = bs.evaluate_design_fast(p, "CTX-0900-S", 3, 2100.0, 85.0, 0.0, 3.0, "DE-2", "SS-304", is_basic=True)
    b_res = compute_lcc(p, b_res)
    basic_lcc = b_res["lcc"]
    print("="*70)
    print(f"PLANT {p}: Basic LCC = ${basic_lcc:,.2f}")
    n_ch = plant["n_ch"]
    best_overall = None

    for n_cells in ([2, 4] if n_ch == 2 else [3, 6]):
        for m_name, m in bs.MODELS.items():
            rects, allow_psf, occ_area = get_valid_siting(p, n_cells, m_name)
            if rects is None: continue
            q_eff = m["q_nom"] * m["cap_mult"]
            gpm_min = max(n_ch * plant["q_cond_min"], n_cells * m["q_min"], n_cells * 0.75 * q_eff)
            gpm_max = min(n_ch * plant["q_cond_max"], n_cells * m["q_max"], n_cells * 1.25 * q_eff, (n_cells - 1) * m["q_max"], (n_cells - 1) * 1.25 * q_eff)
            if gpm_min > gpm_max: continue

            gpm_list = sorted(list(set([gpm_min, gpm_max, round(0.5*(gpm_min+gpm_max))] + [math.ceil(gpm_min/25)*25 + 25*k for k in range(int((gpm_max-gpm_min)//25)+1)])))
            best_combo = None
            for gpm in gpm_list:
                if not (gpm_min <= gpm <= gpm_max): continue
                for cws_min in [plant["cws_min_F"] + 2.5*k for k in range(int((85.0 - plant["cws_min_F"])//2.5)+1)]:
                    for cws_off in [4.0, 5.0, 6.0, 7.0, 8.0, 9.0, 10.0]:
                        for mat in ["SS-304", "FRP-PV"]:
                            res = bs.evaluate_design_fast(p, m_name, n_cells, gpm, cws_min, cws_off, None, "DE-2", mat, is_basic=False)
                            if not res: continue
                            if res["peak_kw"] > plant["mcc_spare_kW"] or res["mk_kgal"] > plant["water_ann_kgal"]: continue
                            res = compute_lcc(p, res, basic_lcc)
                            res["rects"] = rects
                            res["allow_psf"] = allow_psf
                            res["occ_area"] = occ_area
                            if best_combo is None or res["net_savings"] > best_combo["net_savings"]:
                                best_combo = res
                            if best_overall is None or res["net_savings"] > best_overall["net_savings"]:
                                best_overall = res
            if best_combo:
                print(f"  {n_cells}x {m_name} ({best_combo['mat']}): GPM={best_combo['gpm']:.0f}, CWSmin={best_combo['cws_min']}, Off={best_combo['cws_off']}, COC={best_combo['coc']:.2f}, LCC=${best_combo['lcc']:,.0f}, NS=${best_combo['net_savings']:,.0f}, PeakKW={best_combo['peak_kw']:.1f}/{plant['mcc_spare_kW']:.1f}, MK={best_combo['mk_kgal']:.0f}/{plant['water_ann_kgal']:.0f}")

    # Fine-tune around best_overall
    m = bs.MODELS[best_overall["model"]]
    n_cells = best_overall["n_cells"]
    q_eff = m["q_nom"] * m["cap_mult"]
    gpm_min = max(n_ch * plant["q_cond_min"], n_cells * m["q_min"], n_cells * 0.75 * q_eff)
    gpm_max = min(n_ch * plant["q_cond_max"], n_cells * m["q_max"], n_cells * 1.25 * q_eff, (n_cells - 1) * m["q_max"], (n_cells - 1) * 1.25 * q_eff)
    base_gpm = best_overall["gpm"]
    base_min = best_overall["cws_min"]
    base_off = best_overall["cws_off"]
    rects, allow_psf, occ_area = best_overall["rects"], best_overall["allow_psf"], best_overall["occ_area"]
    for dg in range(-50, 55, 5):
        gpm = min(max(base_gpm + dg, gpm_min), gpm_max)
        for dm in [-2.0, -1.5, -1.0, -0.5, 0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0]:
            cws_min = max(plant["cws_min_F"], base_min + dm)
            for doff in [-1.5, -1.0, -0.5, 0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5]:
                cws_off = max(0.0, base_off + doff)
                for mat in ["SS-304", "FRP-PV"]:
                    res = bs.evaluate_design_fast(p, best_overall["model"], n_cells, gpm, cws_min, cws_off, None, "DE-2", mat, is_basic=False)
                    if not res: continue
                    if res["peak_kw"] > plant["mcc_spare_kW"] or res["mk_kgal"] > plant["water_ann_kgal"]: continue
                    res = compute_lcc(p, res, basic_lcc)
                    res["rects"] = rects
                    res["allow_psf"] = allow_psf
                    res["occ_area"] = occ_area
                    if res["net_savings"] > best_overall["net_savings"]:
                        best_overall = res

    SELECTED[p] = best_overall
    print(f"*** SELECTED {p}: {best_overall['n_cells']}x {best_overall['model']} ({best_overall['mat']}), GPM={best_overall['gpm']:.0f}, CWSmin={best_overall['cws_min']}, Off={best_overall['cws_off']}, COC={best_overall['coc']:.2f}, LCC=${best_overall['lcc']:,.2f}, NS=${best_overall['net_savings']:,.2f} ***")

for p in ["CUP", "ANNEX", "LAB"]:

    ws_od = wb.create_sheet("OffDesign")
    ws_od.append([

        "CWFlow_gpm", "AirFlowRatio", "FanPLR", "Range_F", "CWS_F", "CWR_F",

    ])
    for r in sel["bin_rows"]:
        ws_od.append([float(x) if idx not in (4, 5) else int(x) for idx, x in enumerate(r)])

    # 3. WaterBalance
    ws_wb = wb.create_sheet("WaterBalance")
    wb_rows = [
        ("EvaporationMethod", "saturated-exit"),
        ("AnnualEvaporation_kgal", float(sel["evap_kgal"])),

for p in ["CUP", "ANNEX", "LAB"]:

    gpm_max_equip = min(n_ch * plant["q_cond_max"], n_cells * m["q_max"], n_cells * 1.25 * q_eff, (n_cells - 1) * m["q_max"], (n_cells - 1) * 1.25 * q_eff)

    MARGIN_DETAILS[p] = margins

DC-02 Mechanical Design Criteria Memorandum - Condenser Water Heat Rejection
Papago Federal Center, Phoenix, Arizona | Revision 3, 14 August 2026 | Sandoval Klee Mechanical Engineers, PC
This memorandum supersedes DC-02 Revision 2 in its entirety. Revision 3 adds the life-cycle cost objective (paragraph 4, EC-01) and the LifeCycleCost sheet of Appendix A.2.
1. Scope
This memorandum states the criteria, conventions and deliverable requirements for the replacement of the condenser water heat rejection plants serving the Courthouse Central Utility Plant (CUP), the Data Annex (ANNEX) and the Laboratory Wing (LAB). The chillers, the condenser water pumps' hydraulic circuits and the electrical distribution are existing or already procured and are not in the scope of this design.
2. Adopted criteria
3. Plants and served loads
Block cooling loads as a function of outdoor dry-bulb temperature are scheduled on M-603. Chiller performance data and condenser water limits are on M-601 and submittal VD-03.
4. Objective
Each plant must be designed for the HIGHEST LIFE-CYCLE NET SAVINGS, relative to the basic design, consistent with every requirement of the adopted criteria and of this memorandum, with the life-cycle cost analysis performed as EC-01 directs under 10 CFR Part 436 Subpart A. It is not the design with the lowest energy, nor the one with the lowest first cost, unless the analysis makes it so.
Annual plant electrical energy - the energy quantity the analysis prices - is the sum over the scenario bins of paragraph 5.3 of the bin hours multiplied by the coincident electrical demand of the chillers, the tower fans and the condenser water pumps of that plant.
5. Climatic and property basis
5.1 Governing station
The climatic basis is the National Centers for Environmental Information Local Climatological Data record of the airport station serving the site, for the three complete calendar years in the project library. That record is the period of record (POR) for every percentile in this memorandum. Only observations whose report type is FM-15 or FM-16 are counted; the daily and monthly summary rows of the record are not observations. Records for any other station in the library are not part of the POR.
5.2 Design outdoor conditions
A percentile design value is the value that was exceeded that percentage of the observations over the entire POR, taken as a single annual population (not a seasonal one). The design outdoor wet-bulb temperature for the heat rejection equipment is the 1.0 percent annual wet-bulb temperature so computed, adjusted as the adopted HVAC criteria require for open cooling towers. The failure-case calculation of paragraph 6.3 uses the wet-bulb basis that the adopted agency facilities standard prescribes for evaporative machines, adjusted the same way. Do not take design values from the cancelled weather-data criteria document.
5.3 Scenario bins
Annual performance is evaluated on scenario bins formed from the POR observations: bin each observation by wet-bulb temperature in 2 deg F bins and by dry-bulb temperature in 5 deg F bins, take the bin condition as the bin mid-points, and scale the bin counts so that the bins total 8760 hours per year. The block load of a bin is the M-603 load at the bin dry-bulb temperature. Where a bin's dry-bulb mid-point would fall below its wet-bulb mid-point, the dry-bulb temperature is taken equal to the wet-bulb mid-point. The bin edges fall at whole multiples of the bin width measured from zero deg F: an observation belongs to the bin whose lower edge is the largest such multiple that does not exceed it, the lower edge belonging to the bin and the upper edge to the next one, so that a bin's mid-point is its lower edge plus half the bin width.
5.4 Freeze protection
A basin heater and heat-traced makeup piping are required only where the 99.6 percent annual dry-bulb temperature computed from the POR is at or below 32 deg F. The design basis must state the computed 99.6 percent dry-bulb temperature and the determination that follows from it.
5.5 Property basis
Moist air properties are those of the psychrometric routines of the reference implementation in the project library (saturation pressure over water, humidity ratio from dry- and wet-bulb, moist air enthalpy and density, and saturation temperature from enthalpy). The barometric pressure is the mean station pressure of the governing POR, not a sea-level or a standard-atmosphere value. Water is taken at 8.33 lb/gal and 1.0 BTU/lb-deg F, so that heat rejection in BTU/h is 500 times the flow in gpm times the range in deg F.
6. Plant configuration and operating conventions
6.1 Cells and controls
All cells of a plant are of one model and one size and carry identical fan, motor, drift eliminator and material selections. Every tower fan motor is driven by a variable frequency drive. The number of cells must be a whole multiple of the number of chillers served.
6.2 Condenser water flow
Each chiller has a dedicated constant-speed condenser water pump. The scheduled design flow is the flow with every chiller running; the flow with n chillers running is n/N of it. The per-chiller flow must lie inside the condenser flow limits of submittal VD-03 and the per-cell flow inside the limits of submittal VD-01.
6.3 Redundancy
The plant must meet its design block load with the largest single cell out of service, at the failure-case wet-bulb basis of paragraph 5.2, with the remaining cells at full fan speed, and at an entering condenser water temperature no warmer than the machines' published maximum (submittal VD-03). This is the cooling robustness performance tier the agency facilities standard requires.
With a cell out of service the design condenser water flow is unchanged - every chiller is still running on its dedicated constant-speed pump (paragraph 6.2) - and it is carried by the cells that remain in service. The flow through each remaining cell in that state must lie inside the per-cell flow limits of submittal VD-01 and inside the water flow rate ratio limits of the performance object (paragraph 6.8). A plant whose remaining cells would have to pass more than that does not meet this requirement, whatever temperature a calculation extrapolated beyond those limits might predict: a cell above its rated distribution capacity and outside the validity envelope of its performance model has no substantiated capability. The clamping described in the second part of paragraph 6.8 applies to the inlet wet-bulb temperature only; it does not apply to the water flow rate ratio, in this case or any other.
6.4 Condenser water pump power
Condenser water pump total head is taken as a fixed static lift plus a friction component that varies with the square of the flow ratio:
    H = H_static + (H_pipe + H_condenser) x (Q / Q_ref)^2        [ft of water]

where Q is the flow through one pump. The per-plant constants are:
6.5 Chiller staging
Chillers stage on in order: the smallest number of machines whose available capacity at the operating leaving chilled water and entering condenser water temperatures meets the block load runs, and the load is divided equally between them.
Available capacity here is the capacity the adopted performance data set makes available at those temperatures: the machine's reference capacity multiplied by its capacity-as-a-function-of-temperature curve evaluated at the operating point, and nothing else. The maximum part load ratio is not part of available capacity. It is a separate published limit - the ceiling on the load a machine that is already running may be given - and it is not applied to the capacity that decides how many machines run.
6.6 Cell staging
Condenser water is distributed to every installed cell unless the resulting per-cell flow would fall below the effective minimum, which is the larger of the submittal's minimum per-cell flow and the flow at which the performance object's minimum water flow rate ratio is reached. Cells are then isolated one at a time until the per-cell flow is at or above the effective minimum. Tower fans of the cells in service modulate together.
6.7 Condenser water supply temperature control
The condenser water supply temperature setpoint is scheduled as a wet-bulb-following reset: the setpoint is the larger of a scheduled floor and the outdoor wet-bulb temperature plus a scheduled offset, and is in no case below the minimum entering condenser water temperature the chillers are rated for. The fans modulate to the setpoint exactly as the reference implementation models a variable speed tower: full speed when the setpoint cannot be met, free convection when the fans are not needed, minimum speed with cycling below that. A condenser water bypass valve holds the setpoint when the tower would otherwise overcool, so the supply temperature never falls below the setpoint.
6.8 Validity of the performance correlation
A cell may not be operated at a water flow rate ratio outside the limits stated in the performance object, because the implementation clamps the ratio there and the capability would not be substantiated. The range, approach and liquid-to-gas ratio limits of the same object apply at every scenario. A design that operates outside them is not accepted.
The inlet air wet-bulb temperature is treated differently, and deliberately. The reference implementation clamps it to the object's stated range before evaluating the correlation, so an outdoor wet bulb at or above the object's maximum is evaluated AT that maximum and is never extrapolated. The design outdoor wet bulb of paragraph 5.2 lands on that maximum at this site. At the design outdoor wet bulb of paragraph 5.2 and the design block load, with every chiller running at the scheduled design flow and the cells in service at full fan speed, the cells must deliver condenser water no warmer than the scheduled design supply temperature (CWSDESIGN), and the chillers must carry the design block load at that entering condenser water temperature. A schedule may be conservative: a CWSDESIGN warmer than the selected cells actually need is acceptable.

The peak coincident electrical demand of a plant is the largest total electrical demand of the chillers, the tower fans and the condenser water pumps operating together, taken over the scenario bins of paragraph 5.3 and over nothing else. It is a maximum over those bins, not a design-day figure: neither the design point of paragraph 6.9 nor the redundancy case of paragraph 6.3 is a scenario bin - they are sizing conditions - and neither enters this maximum. Basin heaters, controls and lighting are not part of it. This is the quantity the motor control centre's spare capacity limits and the quantity the calculation workbook reports.

The water balance, the cycles of concentration and the treatment programme are governed by the adopted water treatment manual and by the reclaimed water correspondence and treatment memorandum in the project library.
Two evaporation formulations are adopted for this project, and they are these two, named so that the choice is between two fully specified methods:
  SATURATED-EXIT - the moist-air method of the reference implementation's tower water-use routine: the outlet air is saturated at the inlet enthalpy plus the water-side heat transfer divided by the air mass flow, and the evaporated mass is the air mass flow times the rise in specific humidity, converted to a volume with the density of water. As the routine computes them, the inlet enthalpy is that of saturated air at the inlet wet-bulb temperature, and the water density is taken at the mean of the inlet dry-bulb and the saturated outlet air temperatures, not below 4 deg C. === correspondence/RFI-034_Response_Retained_Loads_MCC.docx
RFI-034 Response - Retained Loads on the Motor Control Centers
Papago Federal Center | Response issued 4 September 2026 | Engineer of Record: Sandoval Klee Mechanical Engineers, PC
Question 1
The Laboratory Wing exhaust fan replacement, a separate contract, connects new exhaust fan motors to MCC-R3 before the heat rejection plant is commissioned. Panel schedule E-601 Revision C was prepared from the field survey of 19 February 2026. Does the spare capacity E-601 states for MCC-R3 account for these motors?
Response 1
No. The three laboratory exhaust fans EF-L7, EF-L8 and EF-L9 were not connected at the time of the survey and are not in the retained existing demand of E-601. Each fan is driven by a 7.5 hp, 4 pole, totally enclosed fan cooled motor with a nominal full-load efficiency of 91.7 percent, through a variable frequency drive with an efficiency of 0.97 at rated load. The fans serve fume hood exhaust and run continuously at full speed and full nameplate load, so they operate coincident with the heat rejection plant at every hour of the year. Add their electrical input to the retained existing demand of MCC-R3 and reduce the spare capacity available to the new heat rejection plant accordingly. The bus rating and the continuous loading limit stated on E-601 are unchanged.
Question 2
Are MCC-R1 and MCC-R2 affected?
Response 2
No. No load has been connected to MCC-R1 or MCC-R2 since the survey, and their spare capacities are as E-601 states.
=== site/PW-LTR-014_Reclaimed_Water_Allocation.docx
PW-LTR-014 Reclaimed Water Allocation and Discharge Limits
Papago Municipal Water and Wastewater Authority | 3 July 2026 | to the General Services Administration, Papago Federal Center
This letter confirms the reclaimed water allocation available to the Papago Federal Center for evaporative heat rejection makeup, and the limits on the discharge of cooling tower blowdown to the sanitary sewer, for the condenser water heat rejection replacement project.
1. Allocation
The per-plant allocations above are firm. They are not transferable between plants and they are not increased by the campus total. An allocation covers all makeup water drawn by that plant: evaporation, drift and blowdown.
2. Peak day
The peak day allocation is tested as twenty-four hours of continuous operation at the plant's design day condition, with the plant controlled as scheduled. The design day condition is the design outdoor wet-bulb temperature, the design block load, and - for a water balance that needs the state of the air rather than only its wet bulb - the highest outdoor dry-bulb temperature the block load schedule tabulates for that plant, which is the dry bulb the design block load is reached at.
3. Discharge
Cooling tower blowdown may be discharged to the sanitary sewer up to the daily limit tabulated above. The limit is tested on the same peak day basis as paragraph 2. Discharge above the limit requires a separate industrial discharge permit, which the Authority will not issue for this facility.
4. Metering
Each plant must be separately metered on the makeup line and on the blowdown line. Meter readings are reported to the Authority monthly.
5. Rates
Reclaimed water delivered for evaporative heat rejection makeup is billed at $1.94 per 1,000 gallons of metered makeup. Cooling tower blowdown discharged to the sanitary sewer is billed at $3.20 per 1,000 gallons of metered blowdown. These are the rates in effect on 1 October 2025.
For planning purposes the Authority forecasts that both rates will increase by 3.5 percent per year in then-current dollars over the next thirty years. The forecast is the Authority's financial plan and includes general inflation.

Plant served | Annual allocation (1,000 gal/yr) | Peak day allocation (gal/day) | Blowdown discharge limit (gal/day)

EC-01 Life-Cycle Cost Analysis Criteria - Condenser Water Heat Rejection Replacement
Papago Federal Center, Phoenix, Arizona | Revision 0, 14 August 2026 | Sandoval Klee Mechanical Engineers, PC for the General Services Administration
1. Governing rule
The tower selection for each plant is an energy and water conservation investment in a Federal building and is selected under the Federal life-cycle cost methodology of 10 CFR Part 436, Subpart A (copy in standards/). The alternative tower selections for a plant are mutually exclusive alternatives for one building energy system. Each plant is designed for the HIGHEST NET SAVINGS, in the sense of 10 CFR 436.18(e) and 436.20, relative to the basic design of paragraph 5, among the designs that meet every requirement of the adopted criteria and of DC-02. Net savings of a design = life-cycle cost of the basic design - life-cycle cost of the design.
2. Base date and analysis basis
The base date of the analysis is 1 October 2025, the first day of the FY2026 base year. The analysis is a constant-dollar analysis at base-date prices with the real discount rate (10 CFR 436.14(a)), using the end-of-year conventions of the tables it takes its factors from.
3. Schedule
The design and construction period is 1 year from the base date; beneficial occupancy of the replaced plants is 1 October 2026. Investment costs are taken as a lump sum at the base date (10 CFR 436.14(f)). Energy, water and operation and maintenance costs begin to accrue at beneficial occupancy, not at the base date (436.14(g)); their present values are found as 10 CFR 436.16(c), 436.17(b) and 436.17(d) direct for costs that begin to accrue after the base date.
4. Discount rate, energy escalation and present-value factors
The discount rate, the projected escalation of energy prices and the present-value factors are those of the Annual Supplement to NIST Handbook 135 in force at the base date, as 10 CFR 436.14(a) and (b) require: the 2025 edition. Its data tables - NIST data release doi:10.18434/mds2-3848 - are in economics/ and govern every rate and factor. The project library holds the text of the 2024 edition (NIST IR 85-3273-39) for its explanation of the tables and the method; the tables and the method are organised the same way in both editions, but every rate, factor and worked-example number printed in the 2024 edition is SUPERSEDED by the 2025 data release and must not be used.
Energy conservation projects use the DOE (FEMP) factors and discount rate, not the OMB Circular A-94 factors, which apply to other Federal investments. The site is in Arizona; the electricity is purchased under the commercial general service schedule of letter UT-01. Take the factors for that location, that sector and that fuel. Use the tables as they are printed, without shifting their base year: the year counts of the tables are years from the base date of this analysis.
5. Basic design
The basic design of 10 CFR 436.20 for each plant is the replacement of the existing cells in kind, operated as the existing plants are operated:
The basic design is evaluated with the same simulation basis, scenario bins, staging and control conventions as a proposed design (DC-02) and priced exactly as a proposed design is priced (paragraph 6). It is a reference for net savings only; it is not required to meet the criteria and it is not a candidate selection.
6. Cost data
The water quantities priced in the analysis are those of the SATURATED-EXIT formulation of DC-02 paragraph 7 - the adopted simulation basis - for the proposed design and the basic design alike, whichever formulation the water balance of the calculation workbook is reported in. The allocation and discharge limits of PW-LTR-014 are checked in the formulation the workbook declares.
7. Study period, replacement and salvage
The study period is set by 10 CFR 436.14(d)(2)(i) for mutually exclusive alternatives, the alternatives being the tower selections VD-01 and VD-05 offer that the adopted criteria admit, with their design service lives from the VD-05 ServiceLife sheet. The study period runs from the base date: the design and construction period of paragraph 3 followed by the service period. A cell placed in service at beneficial occupancy with a service life shorter than the service period is replaced when its life expires, at the installed price of one cell as VD-05 states it; the plant controls item is not replaced. Salvage value at the end of the study period is straight-line: the replacement cost multiplied by the unexpired fraction of the service life of the equipment then in service. Replacement and salvage are single amounts discounted from the year in which they occur.
8. Reporting
Each plant's calculation workbook carries the LifeCycleCost sheet of DC-02 Appendix A.2 with the parameters and results of this analysis for the design as scheduled.

1. Introduction  
This report provides tables of present-value factors for use in the life-cycle cost analysis of 
capital investment projects for federal facilities, including energy efficiency, water conservation, 
sustainability, and resilience. It also provides energy price indices based on Department of 
Energy (DOE) forecasts from 2023 to 2050. The factors and indices presented in this report are 
useful for determining the present value of future project-related costs, especially those related 
to operational energy costs. Discount factors included in this report are based on two different 
federal sources: (1) the DOE discount rate for projects related to energy conservation, 
renewable energy resources, and water conservation; and (2) Office of Management and 
Budget (OMB) discount rates from Circular A-94 for use with most other capital investment 
projects in federal facilities. 
The DOE discount and inflation rates for 2023 are as follows: 
Real rate (excluding general price inflation):   
 3.0 % 
Nominal rate (including general price inflation):  
 4.2 % 
Implied long-term average rate of inflation:                1.2 % 
 
The DOE nominal discount rate is based on long-term Treasury bond rates averaged in the 
previous year (2023). The nominal, or market, rate is converted to a real rate to correspond 
with the constant-dollar analysis approach used in most federal life-cycle cost (LCC) analyses. 
The method for calculating the real discount rate from the nominal discount rate is described in 
10 CFR 436 and uses the 10-year simple average projected rates of general inflation published 
in the most recent Report of the President’s Economic Advisors, Analytical Perspectives (2.9 % 
for 2024).1 The procedure would result in a real discount rate for 2024 of 1.3 %, which is lower 
than the 3.0 % floor prescribed in 10 CFR 436.  
Thus the 3.0 % floor is used as the real discount rate for FEMP analyses in 2024. The implied 
long-term average rate of inflation based on the real discount rate (3.0 %) and nominal discount 
rate (4.2 %) was calculated as 1.2 %. Federal agencies and contractors to federal agencies are 
required by 10 CFR 436 to use the DOE discount rates when conducting LCC analyses related to 
energy conservation, renewable energy resources, and water conservation projects for federal 
facilities. 
The nominal and real discount rates applicable to general (non-energy or water) capital 
investments are published annually in OMB Circular A-94, Appendix C.2 OMB has specified two 
basic types of discount rates: (1) a discount rate for public investment and regulatory analyses; 
and (2) a discount rate for cost-effectiveness, lease-purchase, and related analyses. Only 
discount rates for the second type of analyses are included in this Annual Supplement, since the 
primary purpose of this report is to support cost-effectiveness studies related to the design and 
operation of federal facilities.

Life cycle costs. 
Life cycle costs are the sum of the 
present values of— 
(a) Investment costs, less salvage val-
ues at the end of the study period;
